# My Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share, I recognize it as a baseline guide, not a binding constraint. Other players will likely exceed it early on.

In the first season, I take slightly above the sustainable share to test whether other players are cooperating or competing. This gives me a sample of their behavior without committing fully to either strategy.

When I observe that other players are holding close to the sustainable share across multiple seasons and the stock remains stable, I recognize this as a strong signal of cooperation. I should match this restraint to preserve the cooperative equilibrium, which benefits all players including me across the remaining seasons.

When the stock visibly declines below 40, I recognize that the window for high catches is closing. At this point, I shift to taking amounts near the sustainable share to stabilize the resource and avoid total depletion. This preserves my ability to catch in remaining seasons rather than racing others to the bottom.

I should not deviate from a successful cooperative pattern in the middle seasons just to gain a small advantage. If I'm already ahead on cumulative score and the resource is stable, continuing to cooperate both preserves that advantage and prevents triggering competitive escalation that would hurt my total score.

When I reach the final season, I can maximize my catch without restraint since there is no future to preserve. However, I should be careful not to deplete the stock completely—I need to account for other players' likely behavior. Taking a large but not catastrophic share (like 40 when sustainable was 10.7 and stock was 96.6) allows me to gain final advantage while avoiding the appearance of malice.

I do not treat early overfishing as sunk cost that justifies continued overfishing. My score that episode is locked in. Future seasons are decided by future choices, so I adjust my strategy based on current stock levels, not past guilt.

The cooperative strategy worked well in this episode: I finished with 96.4 by staying near sustainable catches for seasons 2-5, then taking a large final catch in season 6. I should default to cooperation early and hold that line unless evidence clearly shows other players are defecting.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I first encounter this game, I'll recognize it as a tragedy of the commons where individual incentives pull against collective welfare.

When I'm tempted to take more than the sustainable share early on, I'll remember that other boats will likely mirror my behavior. If I take 20 when sustainable is 11, they'll take 20 too, and the stock will collapse rapidly, ending everyone's catches prematurely.

When I see others taking more than sustainable, I won't assume this justifies my own overfishing. Matching their greed accelerates the commons collapse. I should instead use their behavior as a signal to adjust my expectations downward, not upward.

When calculating my strategy, I'll project the full game forward. I'll see that taking the sustainable share every season yields roughly 66 total per boat over 6 seasons, while aggressive early catches followed by stock depletion yields less overall.

When I'm ahead on individual score, I won't use that as justification to stay aggressive. Being ahead now means little if the fishery collapses before the final seasons.

When I reach the final season, I'll resist the logic that "there's no future to preserve." Squeezing out an extra 0.7 fish on season 6 isn't worth abandoning the sustainable path. I should stick to sustainable levels consistently.

When the stock is exactly at equilibrium and other boats are taking their sustainable share, I'll take mine too. This is the winning strategy.

When I overshoot the sustainable share early (as I did in season 1), I'll course-correct immediately. Taking more than sustainable signals aggression and risks triggering defection from others. Returning to sustainable levels quickly reasserts commitment to cooperation before the cascade begins.

When I'm tempted to deviate late in the game, I'll remember that even one defection in the final seasons can break the equilibrium. The other boats are watching consistency. If I've been sustainable for 4-5 seasons, abandoning it now teaches them that cooperation was a mistake, and they may defect if we play again.

When calculating total payoff, I'll account for the full 6 seasons, not partial scenarios. My actual result of 64.9 by maintaining near-sustainable catches throughout demonstrates that steady cooperation outperforms early aggression even accounting for minor overfishing in season 1.

My next game: I will take the sustainable share from season one without deviation and maintain it throughout all six seasons, trusting that consistent cooperation maximizes my total score better than any defection strategy.

# My Playbook for the Commons Fishery Game

When I see the sustainable catch rate, I treat it as a genuine guideline, not a ceiling to be exploited.

When I'm deciding my opening catch, I remember that aggressive early fishing (catching significantly above the sustainable share) damages the stock severely and limits everyone's total haul over the full game. I will catch at or near the sustainable rate from Season 1.

When I observe other boats' catches, I recognize that if they're fishing above sustainable levels, the stock will collapse faster, harming me more than it helps. I don't use their behavior to justify my own overexploitation.

When I deviate from the sustainable rate early (as I did by catching 13.0 when the rate was 11.1 in Season 1), I acknowledge this immediately and course-correct in the very next season. One bad decision doesn't justify continued overexploitation. Returning to sustainable fishing limits the total damage.

When the stock falls below half its starting value, I acknowledge I've already contributed to degradation and shift decisively to sustainable fishing for the remainder of the game.

When I'm tempted to catch above the sustainable share on the grounds that "it's the last season so consequences don't matter," I remember that my final score is the sum of all seasons. One large grab in the final season doesn't offset the damage to the overall pool.

When I'm tracking my cumulative catch versus the sustainable path, I recognize being ahead early as a warning sign, not a victory. It signals overexploitation.

When I see other boats demonstrating restraint and cooperation, I join that pattern rather than exploit it. Cooperation preserves the stock and my long-term score.

When the stock stabilizes near its starting value over multiple seasons while I fish at the sustainable rate, I recognize this as confirmation that the strategy works. This pattern is a reliable signal to maintain discipline through the final season.

I will aim to catch the sustainable share every single season. Over six seasons at the sustainable rate, my score will be stable and respectable—approximately 64-65 fish. Deviations above that rate, even modest ones, cascade into stock collapse that costs me far more than I gain.
